text: distribution and behavior of the Embiotocidae in a 3800
square meter section of the protected nearshore zone at Point
Cabrillo, California (see figure 1). I used snorkeling and
occasionally SCUBA diving gear and recorded my counts and
observations on underwater paper. Observations were
conducted at different times during the day and tidal cycle.
The study area was divided into five separate habitats; the
time spent in each was recorded and remained fairly constant
for each respective area. A structured pattern was followed
on each snorkel survey in order to avoid as much repetitive
counting of individuals as possible.
Habitat A (370 square meters), the area under and around
the railroad tracks, is very well-protected from surge and
breaking waves by Seal Rocks. Phyliospadix covers the
shallow intertidal area of the tracks; algae grows all over
the submerged tracks and ties which are approximately one
foot above the sandy bottom. The area slopes down to a depth
of 10-15 feet, where the tracks end and a small grove of
Macrocystis begins. I usually spent 15 minutes here.
Habitat B (1600 square meters), the area protected by
Seal Rocks, is marked on its southern boundary by a sand
channel. The bottom is characterized by medium-sized and
large rocks, thick Phyliospadix, and sandy patches. Other
than the sandy, shallow area near the shore, the approximate
depth of this habitat ranges from 4 to 8 feet. Surge is
greater in this area than at the railroad tracks, but rarely
strong. This is a popular swimming area for harbor seals.
My observation time here was about 30 minutes.
